extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature and literary criticism; playwrights/students studying Aristotelian tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing or composing tragedy according to Aristotle's Poetics: defining features (mimesis, seriousness, completeness, magnitude), required emotional effects (pity and fear), and the katharsis that tragedy must produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy (Aristotle)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper katharsis, or purgation, of these emotions.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This single sentence bundles the chief formal and functional requirements: mimesis (imitation), seriousness, completeness, magnitude, ornamental language (verse/song placed appropriately), dramatic (acted) form rather than narrative, and the aesthetic aim of producing katharsis through pity and fear. Use this definition as the checklist for whether a work counts as Aristotelian tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis (imitation) as the genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy belongs to the genus of imitation (mimesis), a feature it shares with other fine arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work should present action by representation (dramatic enactment) rather than abstract discussion. Emphasize showing rather than telling; enact causes and effects through characters' actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness (σπουδαίας)
rubrics_metrics.description: The action imitated must be 'serious' (σπουδαίας): neither ludicrous (γελοῖα) nor morally trivial (φαύλη).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seriousness means grave and great in tone and import; avoid mere comic or petty material. Note: 'noble' is an imperfect translation—σπουδαίας conveys both grave quality and a contrast to comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness / unity of action (τελείας)
rubrics_metrics.description: The action should be complete (having a beginning, middle, and end) — a fully unified and self-contained action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the plot has a coherent causal sequence that comes to a proper conclusion; avoid disjointed episodic or fragmentary structures that fail to form a single integrated action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (μέγεθος) — appropriate scope/length
rubrics_metrics.description: The action must be of a certain magnitude: an appropriate size or extent (which may refer to actual length/duration and to significance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnitude concerns both the temporal span and the weight/significance of the action. Do not conflate it with mere wordy length; choose a scope that permits full development of the unified action and its tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form: dramatic action, not narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must be presented in the form of action (dramatic performance) rather than by narrative (epic/story-telling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer enacted scenes and dialogue to long authorial summaries; the tragic effect depends on spectators witnessing events as they unfold, not being told about them after the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embellishments: appropriate use of verse and song
rubrics_metrics.description: Language should be 'embellished with each kind of artistic ornament' — verse and lyrical song, with verse (without music) for dialogue and lyrical song for choral parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute artistic ornaments according to dramatic function: dialogues in metrical verse, choral odes as sung/lyrical elements. This distinguishes tragedy from other poetic forms (e.g., nomic or dithyrambic) which combine embellishments throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary tragic emotions: pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic spectacle must excite the specific aesthetic emotions of pity (ἔλεος) and fear (φόβος); these are the 'aforesaid emotions' with which tragedy is concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design incidents and character relations that elicit compassion for undeserved suffering and a sympathetic shudder of fear—not generalized sorrow or terror for unrelated reasons. Other emotions may appear, but pity and fear are central to tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Katharsis (the function/purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy's proper function is to effect a katharsis (purgation) of the tragic emotions (pity and fear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations vary: (a) medical/pathological (Bernays): katharsis as a homoeopathic, pleasurable relief—excitement followed by discharge; (b) moral/purificatory: removal of morbid elements and clarification of feeling; (c) aesthetic: transformation of base passions into refined, pleasurable calm. In crafting tragedy aim to produce an aesthetic purification or relief in the audience through the structured arousal and resolution of pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of katharsis: purgation and clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: Katharsis involves expelling the morbid, disturbing element from pity and fear and purifying these emotions into higher, clarified forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work towards dramatizing suffering so that the painful or selfish element in pity/fear is relinquished; the audience's feelings should be 'transmuted' and 'universalised' rather than merely vented. Avoid depictions that leave only raw, unprocessed sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character's moral likeness (ὅμοιος) to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero must be 'like us' in moral nature (ὅμοιος) so that spectators can identify and feel fear on his behalf; identification depends on moral resemblance rather than exact social parity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray heroes with human virtues and frailties so the audience can sympathize; the hero's moral likeness—not merely external similarity—elicits the sympathetic shudder that constitutes tragic fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero's status: elevated yet fallible (not flawless or villainous)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should be raised above common life in dignity or station (e.g., a prince or famous person) but not morally perfect nor utterly villainous; he should possess human frailties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a figure of stature to provide distance and universalising effect, but give him errors or imperfections that ground his fall and make pity and fear possible. Avoid making the hero wholly monstrous or merely average and domestic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of pity: the undeserving (ἀνάξιος)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pity, as Aristotle employs it, is felt for one who is undeserving (ὁ ἀνάξιος) — i.e., a sufferer who meets with misfortune beyond his deserts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct suffering that appears disproportionate or undeserved to evoke genuine pity; avoid situations where the audience perceives the suffering as deserved, which would undermine pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined appeal to both pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper tragedy engages both pity and fear together rather than one alone; the combined effect is what leads to the katharsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plot developments that alternately foreground undeserved suffering (pity) and close moral resemblance/impending calamity (fear), so that the interplay of the two builds to a purgative resolution. Beware plays that elicit only one emotion and thus fail to achieve full tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic fear is sympathetic, not direct self-fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic φόβος differs from real-life fear: it is a sympathetic shudder toward a hero who is similar to us rather than an immediate fear that the same disaster will befall ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage situations to produce vicarious apprehension—the audience experiences fear through identification with the hero's moral condition rather than literal anticipation of identical fate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement/universalisation of emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under artistic conditions, pity and fear are disengaged from petty self-interest and universalised; tragedy refines lower emotions into higher aesthetic satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for representations that elevate the spectator's feelings—remove immediate personal anxieties and present the emotions in a form that conveys general human significance. Avoid overly intimate or quotidian details that trap the audience in mundane self-concern.
